say.text: A cyanotic 4-month-old has echo-confirmed TOF. Before we read anything off the tracing, a quick prediction.
Which ECG pattern fits?

choices.label: Left axis deviation with a left ventricular hypertrophy pattern
Right axis deviation with a right ventricular hypertrophy pattern
Left atrial enlargement with a left ventricular hypertrophy pattern
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which ventricle faces the obstruction in TOF. The tracing reflects the chamber that is working hardest.
Yes. The ECG in TOF shows right axis deviation, prominent R or qR waves in V1 and upright T waves in V1, characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH).

'Hypertrophy' without a side feels like the left ventricle, the chamber we meet most often. In TOF the tracing is right-sided: right axis deviation, prominent R or qR in V1, upright T in V1 (right atrial enlargement and RVH).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look. Name the side first, then pick the chamber and axis.

say.text: Left-sided enlargement is the familiar answer to a strained heart, so it tempts. TOF reads the other way round: the ECG is characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy, with right axis deviation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look. Name the side first, then pick the chamber and axis.

say.text: Worked example. Steps 1 and 2, which you just reasoned: the RV pumps against the narrowed outflow, RVH follows, secondary to chronic systemic pressures, and the tracing turns right-sided.
Step 3. With significant RVOT (right ventricular outflow tract) obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta and bypasses the pulmonary bed.
Same infant, chest X-ray now. Follow the blood that leaves the right ventricle against a narrowed outflow, with a VSD beside it.
What do the lung fields look like?

choices.label: Plethoric, because the VSD floods the lungs
Normal fields, but with marked cardiomegaly
Oligaemic, because blood bypasses the pulmonary bed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Follow the blood. If most of it goes to the aorta, how much is left to reach the lung vessels?
Right. Most blood goes toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed, so the film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings.

A VSD sounds like a lung-flooding shunt, so plethora is tempting. Here the RVOT obstruction sends most blood toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed. The lungs can show decreased markings, not plethora.

say.text: Think back to the ECG: which chamber is thick in TOF?
Yes. The upturned apex is attributed to RVH, together with a concave pulmonary arterial segment.
The left ventricle is the usual suspect for an enlarged apex. In TOF the apex is lifted by RVH, with a concave pulmonary arterial segment.

say.text: A big pulmonary artery would make a bulge, so it feels plausible. The film shows a concave pulmonary arterial segment, and the apex is upturned because of RVH.

say.text: Fade three, no scaffold. Your colleague says: 'No boot-shaped heart on this film, so it cannot be TOF.'
Reading the wording of the source, what is the fair response?

choices.label: Agreed: the boot-shaped heart is always present in TOF
Films may classically show a boot; it is not guaranteed
Agreed: the boot is the film sign that confirms TOF
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the exact verb the source uses for this sign, and ask what that verb allows.
Yes. Chest radiographs may classically show a boot-shaped heart. 'May' makes it a classic possibility, not a requirement.
'Classic' tempts us to read 'always'. The wording is that radiographs may classically show a boot-shaped heart, so it is not guaranteed.

say.text: Tempting, because the boot is the best-known film sign. But a film sign does not confirm the diagnosis.
Radiographs may classically show the boot; the echocardiogram is the gold standard for diagnosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two jobs: the film may show a classic sign, echo is the gold standard.

say.text: Last film question. A radiologist describes the film.
Which description fits TOF?

choices.label: Egg-on-a-string heart with a narrow pedicle
Normal-sized heart, upturned apex, oligaemic lung fields
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. StatPearls describes a normal-size heart with an upturned apex, and the lungs can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
A named film sign feels like a good match from a memorised list. Build the TOF film from physiology instead: a normal-size silhouette, upturned apex from RVH, oligaemic lungs.
Cardiomegaly with plethora is the pattern we expect when lungs are flooded. In TOF the film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings and a normal-size heart.
The film and ECG fit, but they do not settle it. A cyanotic 2-month-old has a harsh ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and right axis deviation.

Yes. Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosis and remains the primary modality, because it allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy.

say.text: Match each test to its question. Diagnosis: echo, as you just saw.
Complex cardiovascular morphology: contrast-enhanced CT.
Anatomy plus function, with no ionising radiation: MRI.

choices.label: Cardiac catheterisation as the gold standard

Yes. Contrast-enhanced CT is useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology of TOF.
Echo is the primary modality, so 'nothing more' feels natural. But CT is described as useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology, which is the extra job here.

choices.label: MRI for first-line diagnosis; echo for follow-up only
Echo for diagnosis; MRI for anatomy plus function without radiation
Catheterisation for diagnosis; echo for screening only

say.text: Yes. Echo is the primary diagnostic modality, and MRI provides anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.

choices.label: Go deeper: what echo can miss

say.text: MRI is detailed and radiation-free, which makes it tempting as first line. But echocardiography is the primary diagnostic modality; MRI adds anatomical and functional information.
Catheterisation feels like the rigorous test. The gold standard for diagnosis is echocardiography, the primary modality.
Echocardiography has limitations in assessing associated extracardiac anomalies such as peripheral pulmonary stenosis and atresia.
Pulmonary artery assessment matters: repairing cardiac defects without addressing pulmonary artery hypoplasia or stenosis has a poor outcome.
The main or right pulmonary artery diameter should be compared with that of the ascending aorta. CT can also evaluate post-surgical changes, such as patency of palliative shunts.
Now explain it. Why is there a right ventricular hypertrophy pattern at all?

choices.label: VSD volume overloads the left ventricle and strains the right
The RV is thick as a primary malformation, present before any load
The RV works against chronic systemic-level pressure, so it thickens
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the right ventricle has been pumping against since birth, and what any muscle does under a long load.
Yes. RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures: it is a consequence of the load, not a primary malformation.

choices.label: Walk me through the chain to the film
I have it, show me the chest film

say.text: Volume overload of the left side is a familiar shunt idea, so it is tempting.
The mechanism here is different: RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures on the RV, a pressure load on the right, not a left-sided volume load.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the ECG follows the right ventricle, the chamber under pressure.

say.text: Calling RVH a defect is tempting because it is one of the four named components.
But RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures: a consequence of the load, not a primary malformation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reverse the arrow: the pressure comes first, the thick right ventricle follows.

say.text: Build the film from your three answers: how big is the heart, which chamber lifts the apex, and how much blood reaches the lungs?
The ladder: the RV faces the block, so the ECG is right-sided (right axis deviation, RVH) and the film is oligaemic with an upturned apex that may classically look boot-shaped.
Echo diagnoses, CT shows morphology, MRI adds function.

cards.a: Right axis deviation, prominent R or qR and upright T in V1: right atrial enlargement and RVH.

cards.q: Why is the RV hypertrophied in TOF?
cards.a: RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.

cards.q: Lung fields on a TOF chest X-ray, and why?
cards.a: Oligaemic: with significant RVOT obstruction most blood shunts to the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.

cards.q: What lifts the apex of the boot-shaped heart, and is the boot always seen?
cards.a: RVH, with a concave pulmonary arterial segment; radiographs may classically show it.

cards.q: Gold standard for diagnosing TOF? What do CT and MRI add?
cards.a: Echocardiography. Contrast CT shows complex morphology; MRI gives anatomy plus function without ionising radiation.
